text.en: Tape loops grew out of records. In late-1940s Paris, the composer Pierre Schaeffer used records with a "closed groove" to repeat bits of sound; when magnetic tape became available, he switched to tape loops.

headline.en: A looper sings a short part, lets it repeat, and sings over it: a band made of one voice. Hear one: a bass four times round, and a second part over it. This course is for the web app for now.

text.en: Reacting to a sound takes about 160 milliseconds on average, a 2013 paper notes, yet trained ensemble musicians typically land 30 to 50 milliseconds apart: too close for reacting alone, which suggests they predict.

source.en: van der Steen and Keller, Frontiers in Human Neuroscience (2013)

text.en: The Mellotron, made in England from 1963, played a strip of recorded tape under each key, with a choir among its sounds. A held note usually lasted about eight seconds before the tape ran out.

source.en: 120 Years of Electronic Music, The Mellotron (Leslie Bradley, UK, 1963)

text.en: Scotland's puirt à beul, "tunes from a mouth", set Gaelic words to dance tunes and were used for dancing when there were no instruments. Their rhythm and sound often matter more than the words' own rhythm.

text.en: A barcarolle, the boat song of Venice's gondoliers, is almost always in 6/8, with a rhythm meant to recall the gondolier's stroke. One of the most famous is in Offenbach's opera The Tales of Hoffmann.

text.en: Drunken Sailor's earliest known printing is in an 1841 whaling book, as just "Ho! Ho! and up she rises... Early in the morning". One man usually struck up the song; the rest joined in.

source.en: Olmsted, Incidents of a Whaling Voyage (1841), Internet Archive

text.en: La Folia, a minor-key chord pattern, is one of Europe's oldest remembered musical themes. Over three centuries, more than 150 composers wrote their own music on its chords.
